field: transformsOf, negate transform, rendered answer for bank:u60-t-word-order-style-0039 (also ¿Raras veces no cocinas tú en casa? from -0025, Contá cómo no te fue con el abogado from u59-1048)
quote: Poco no me sirvió, la verdad.
problem: The generator produces exactly the error that g:word-order-style lists as a pitfall (Poco no importa ya: "a double negative that Spanish does not use here") and accepts it as correct. The negate transform inserts no before the first finite verb without knowing that poco and raras veces already carry negative force, or that the negation in Contá cómo te fue belongs on the imperative.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009), on anteposed negative-polarity quantifiers

quote: Normal order puts the subject first: *El barrio ha cambiado mucho.*
problem: With verbs of arriving, appearing and remaining, the subject normally follows: se fue la luz, llegó Vale, queda poco. The lesson's own examples (Poco queda del edificio) have no subject to move. This is the last word-order lesson in the course and the only one a C1 learner gets; subject after the verb when the subject is the news is taught nowhere.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on subject position and informational focus; Bosque and Demonte, Gramatica descriptiva
replacement: With most verbs the subject comes first: *El barrio ha cambiado mucho.* With verbs like *llegar*, *quedar* and *faltar* it usually follows, because it is the news: *llegó Vale*.

authority: tested with matchTranslation and checkExact
replacement: Put the key word first: It's hard to say.

field: transformsOf, tense transform, rendered answer for bank:u53-0542
quote: Ayer Cada uní con su cuento: ese es el barrio.
problem: The clause parser reads the pronoun uno as first person of unir and conjugates it to uní. Other wrong outputs from the same survey of all 13,410 C1 rows: Antes Gracias, tenía razón. (u53-1645); Ayer de ser así, fuimos a juicio. (u53-0882); Antes Cada quien sabía lo suyo y calla lo ajeno. (u53-0543, half the sentence shifted). 349 of 2,126 Antes or Ayer answers leave a capital on the second word.
authority: morphology: uno is a pronoun here

quote: You only need to recognise it, never to say it.
problem: The script promises recognition only, and the owner's standing decision is no voseo, but nothing in the compiler treats this node as receptive. In 8 rendered days at u59 the learner gets 20 "How do you say this in Spanish?" cards ending in (vos) and must type answers such as Vos sos el único que me entiende. All 126 rows have an empty accept list, so the tú form the script tells them to use is marked wrong.
authority: owner standing decision; rendered with tools/playtest/render.ts 59 8

quote: The *tú* commands are *ven* and *siéntate*: the *d* disappears from *vení*.
problem: Vení has no d. The sentence appears to have been built from Spain's venid.
authority: orthography
replacement: The *tú* commands are *ven* and *siéntate*: *vení* loses its last vowel and *sentate* gets its *ie* back.

quote: Vale does it all the time when she is happy or angry.
problem: False. Across all 219 chapters the only voseo word is the wrong option Que aprenda a hablar de vos in a ch213 question, and the 270 scenes have none. Vale speaks tú throughout (ch184: Conmigo dices las cosas que son tuyas).
authority: measured with a search over app/content/story and app/content/scenes

quote: You will hear it all through Vale's story.
problem: Same false promise. Either add paisa voseo to the Medellín chapters at the end of the course, which is the stronger option, or remove the claim.
authority: measured

quote: Commands also put the stress at the end: *vení* (*ven*), *sentate* (*siéntate*).
problem: Rows use forms this rule never prepares: Vos sabés que acá siempre hay un plato para vos, Vos te enredás cuando hablás rápido, Sí, tomá. The learner needs to know vos follows prepositions and the object pronoun stays te.
authority: measured against bank rows; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: Commands also put the stress at the end: *vení* (*ven*), *sentate* (*siéntate*). After a preposition it stays *vos* (*para vos*, *con vos*), and the object word stays *te*: *¿vos te acordás?*

quote: So: read it, understand it as "if or whoever, later", and never use it yourself.
problem: The learner is then required to type it. Rendered at u60: "Those who live in the area will receive a notice." with the answer Quienes vivieren en la zona recibirán un aviso. All 127 rows have an empty accept list, so the correct modern Spanish Quienes vivan en la zona... is rejected in favour of a form the script forbids.
authority: rendered with tools/playtest/render.ts 60 8; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive as archaic outside legal language

quote: Quien bien amare, tarde olvidará.
problem: The saying is Quien bien ama, tarde olvida. The -re version is invented and presented as a proverb, and u59-1206 attributes it to Hernando's grandfather.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Quien quisiere celeste, que le cueste, decía mi tío.
problem: The saying is Quien quiera celeste, que le cueste. The archaic form is invented.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Si algún día tuviere una hija, le pondré Rosa.
problem: A personal promise in the future subjunctive. pitfalls[2] says of this very use: "No one talks this way."
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Cuando el café estuviere listo, avisaré a todos.
problem: Everyday context, same contradiction with pitfalls[2].
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: Si te vieres en problemas, escríbeme.
problem: Informal tú to a friend, same contradiction with pitfalls[2].
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on the future subjunctive; paremiology by usage

quote: De haber llegado antes, habríamos visto a Hernando.
problem: The checker has no equivalence for forms that are fully interchangeable in standard Spanish. Tested and rejected: De haber llegado antes, hubiéramos visto a Hernando. against this answer; El hecho de que no llamase me preocupa. against -ra. Hubiera in the result clause is at least as common as habría in Latin American speech, so a learner who writes correct Bogotá Spanish is marked wrong.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry on haber and the -ra form in the apodosis; Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish
replacement: Add two global variants to expandAccepted: -ra and -se in any imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive, and habría + participle with hubiera + participle in the main clause of a past unreal condition.

quote: What follows is never a new fact. It is the first fact, made clearer.
problem: The script's own examples break this. Es caro; o sea, no lo podemos pagar and Hernando viene todos los días; o sea, conoce el café mejor que nadie add a conclusion, not a restatement. O sea and es decir both work as conclusive markers. A learner who believes the rule cannot explain half the examples and will not recognise the most frequent spoken use.
authority: Diccionario de particulas discursivas del espanol, entry o sea; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009)
replacement: What follows is the first idea made clearer, or what it comes down to.

quote: Hernando comes every day; I mean, he knows the café better than anyone.
problem: This o sea is conclusive, so "I mean" misrenders it. The natural English is "so".
authority: semantic reasoning
replacement: Hernando comes every day, so he knows the café better than anyone.

quote: I arrived late, I mean, I missed the speech.
problem: Conclusive o sea. Missing the speech follows from arriving late, it does not restate it.
authority: semantic reasoning
replacement: I arrived late, so I missed the speech.

quote: Note the *que* in *o sea que*: no *que*, no conclusion.
problem: False, and contradicted by g:reformulation, taught the day before: Es caro; o sea, no lo podemos pagar is a conclusion with no que. Also Llegué tarde; o sea, me perdí el discurso (u53-1223).
authority: Diccionario de particulas discursivas del espanol, entry o sea
replacement: Note the *que*: *o sea que* runs straight into the sentence, with no comma. *O sea* on its own takes a comma: *o sea, Tomás se queda*.

quote: Almost. To draw a conclusion with a full sentence, *o sea* needs its *que*.
problem: O sea, Tomás se queda is correct. What is wrong in the pitfall sentence is the missing comma or que, not the lack of que as such.
authority: punctuation norm; usage evidence
replacement: Almost. Join it with *que*, or put a comma after *o sea*.

quote: Ask yourself: pointed at, or still open?
problem: The model fails the script's first example. El hecho de que no llamara is a fact you can point to, and the script says so ("The fact isn't in doubt"), yet it takes the subjunctive. A learner applying the closing test gets the indicative. The better model already exists in this band: g:consecutive-advanced says de ahí que takes the subjunctive "because you are not announcing the result as news". That one axis covers lo que digas, el hecho de que, aunque seas and de ahí que.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009), on the indicative as assertion and the subjunctive as non-assertion
replacement: Ask yourself: am I putting this forward as news? News takes the indicative. Everything else takes the subjunctive: what is still open, and what is already known and you are only reacting to.

quote: El hecho de que no llamó me preocupa.
problem: The perfect subjunctive, probably the most natural form here for a recent event, is rejected. Tested with matchTranslation. The indicative, which the script calls the unusual choice, is accepted.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on subjunctive tense after a present main verb
replacement: accept: ["El hecho de que no llamó me preocupa.", "El hecho de que no haya llamado me preocupa."]

quote: *Como no vengas, me enojo* means *if you don't come, I'll get angry*.
problem: This is the striking half of the lesson and the title names it, but como + subjunctive appears only in this rule line. It is in no example, Read and Pick or Your Turn, so the indicative and subjunctive como are never contrasted.
authority: measured: no como + subjunctive in examples, readAndPick or yourTurn
replacement: Add to examples, readAndPick and yourTurn: Como no vengas, me enojo. = If you don't come, I'll get angry. (to a friend)

quote: Teachers call these conditional clauses without *si*: *de* + compound infinitive, *como* + subjunctive, and the connectors *a no ser que* and *con tal de que*.
problem: Conditional como + subjunctive is much more typical of Spain than of Colombia, where si no vienes is the everyday form. The course gives it to Bogotá speakers with no regional note (ch202: Como no respire, mija, se me desmaya; Y como alguien me ponga corbata, me levanto). A learner will take it for the normal local threat.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish; RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009); confidence limited, no corpus access
replacement: Teachers call these conditional clauses without *si*: *de* + compound infinitive, *como* + subjunctive, and the connectors *a no ser que* and *con tal de que*. *Como* with the subjunctive is more common in Spain; in Colombia most people would say *si no llegas*.

quote: The result usually uses *habría*.
problem: Hubiera is equally standard in the result clause and very common in Latin America, and the story itself uses an imperfect (ch202: De haber tenido más tiempo, traíamos a los de Medellín).
authority: RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry on haber; usage evidence
replacement: The result uses *habría* or *hubiera*.

quote: De haber llegado antes habríamos visto a Hernando.
problem: De haber llegado antes, hubiéramos visto a Hernando is rejected (tested). A global checker variant is the better fix; this is the content-level stopgap.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas
replacement: accept: ["De haber llegado antes habríamos visto a Hernando.", "De haber llegado antes, hubiéramos visto a Hernando."]

quote: *De* + *haber* + *-ado/-ido* looks back: *de haberlo sabido*, "had I known".
problem: De + simple infinitive, the commoner form, is left out: de ser así, de seguir así, de no ser por. The course knows de ser así as a chunk (u53-1926) but never connects it.
authority: RAE and ASALE, Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (2009) on condicionales de infinitivo
replacement: *De* + *haber* + *-ado/-ido* looks back: *de haberlo sabido*, "had I known". *De* + the plain verb looks at now or next: *de ser así*, "if so".

quote: Conditions with style: de haberlo sabido, como no llegues, a no ser que, siempre y cuando
problem: The script never contains siempre y cuando. It says "four ways" and teaches de haber, como, a no ser que and con tal de que.
authority: measured
replacement: Conditions with style: de haberlo sabido, como no llegues, a no ser que, con tal de que

quote: Conditions with style: de haberlo sabido, como no llegues, a no ser que, siempre y cuando
problem: The title promises siempre y cuando, but the script's rule, examples and pitfalls teach con tal de que instead. Either teach it or change the title.
authority: Script g_conditional-advanced.json
replacement: Conditions with style: de haberlo sabido, como no llegues, a no ser que, con tal de que
